newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British factory-gate prices edge higher.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British factory-gate prices edge higher.

text.p: British factory-gate prices edged higher in October, largely due to a surge in oil prices, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on Monday.
City economists said the figures indicated a modest increase in inflationary pressure in the pipeline but they were not a serious cause for concern.

The ONS said output prices -- the price of goods leaving factory gates -- rose 0.2 percent in October, giving a year-on-year increase of 2.3 percent compared with 2.2 percent in the year to September.
Input prices, a measure of the costs of raw materials and fuel, rose by a seasonally-adjusted 0.5 percent in October but were down two percent from a year earlier.
"All of the rise in input prices was due to the recent rises in oil prices -- crude oil prices are 44 percent higher than a year ago," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.

Although other components either fell or were flat, Loynes said the rise in oil prices threatened to put further upward pressure on underlying inflation in the next few months, pushing it further away from the government's target of 2.5 percent.

"Oil apart, cost pressures in industry remain extremely subdued suggesting that, while the next few inflation figures will be pushed up by higher petrol prices, the underlying picture continues to look favourable," he added.

Underlying inflation, which excludes volatile mortgage interest payments, rose to 2.9 percent in September after being stuck at 2.8 percent for four months. October figures will be released on Thursday.
Economists said Monday's figures were not strong enough to prompt the Bank of England to step up pressure for a further rise in official interest rates in the near future.

Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke bowed to pressure from the Bank and raised rates unexpectedly on October 30 to six percent from 5.75 percent to head off a future pickup in inflation.
Speaking in Basle on Monday before the producer price data were released, Bank of England Governor Eddie George said a further rate rise would probably be needed.
"But the fact that we moved early is extremely helpful," he told reporters. "It certainly serves to limit the rise that may ultimately become necessary."
Economists said input prices could ease further in the next few months as the strong pound makes imports cheaper.

"Non-oil commodity prices have dropped sharply in recent weeks in sterling terms and this will help to dampen input prices in coming months -- subsequently feeding through to cap output prices and retail prices as well," said Michael Saunders, an economist at Salomon Brothers.
